entry.title: Is Credit Assignment Outdated?
entry.content:
A few days ago I published Why Do Chinese LLMs Struggle with RL?, and its version on Xiaohongshu (RedNote) drew more than a hundred comments. One kind of reply kept coming back. Hardly anyone uses a critic any more, it went; the leading labs have dropped PPO, and some have gone back to the simpler REINFORCE. A critic works at small scale but does not fit how things scale up. A critic has to predict the future, which may be harder than solving the task itself. Someone also said that if one RL trajectory takes days to run, you should not do RL on that task at all and just use SFT. Follow these remarks to their end and you arrive at one conclusion, that long-horizon credit assignment is outdated. Nor is this view confined to the comments; plenty of people in the field think credit assignment is no longer useful, that its time has passed.

Let me put it plainly. There is no such thing as credit assignment going out of date. Calling it outdated may sound like standing at the frontier, but it confuses a problem with a method, and in RL that is an elementary mistake. It is a problem that is always there in RL, and the only things that change are how hard it is to solve and whether it needs solving in its own right. The era of long-horizon tasks and agents is exactly when it most needs solving in its own right.

First, a little background, which readers who know it can skip. When RL trains a large model, the model gets a single score only after it finishes a whole task. Credit assignment is the question of which steps deserve the credit, or the blame, once that task has succeeded or failed.

Problem and Methods

What those remarks call outdated is really specific methods such as PPO and the critic. Methods do go out of date. The problem does not. As long as a model gets one score only after finishing a whole task, that score has to be shared out among the steps somehow.

GRPO does not get around the problem either. It compares the score of a whole trajectory with the group’s average and hands that difference, unchanged, to every token. If the attempt was right, every step is reinforced together; if it was wrong, every step is penalized together. This is the coarsest way to split the score, but it is still a way to split it.

So “no critic” means a different way of splitting, not that the problem went away. Nor were the critic, process supervision and PPO ever tied together. PPO falling out of fashion does not make the critic useless, still less credit assignment. Tying a problem to one method, then declaring the problem outdated because the method is out of fashion, is a step of reasoning that does not hold.

The Short-Horizon Era

Not solving it in its own right does not mean the problem is absent. It only means that in that period it was easy, and a coarse split was enough. On this point, much of what those remarks say is right.

First, on short-horizon tasks such as math problems, there are very few places where a real choice is made. Wang et al., in a 2025 paper, looked at the entropy of each token in a reasoning trace, that is, how unsure the model is at that position, and found that only about a fifth of the tokens have high entropy. These tokens are like forks in the road and decide which way the reasoning goes, while the other four fifths mostly just carry on. Updating only that fifth matched updating every token on an 8B model and did clearly better on 14B and 32B. With few forks and a short road, even an equal split gives each fork a large enough share.

Second, sampling is cheap. A math problem is done quickly, and attempting the same problem dozens of times costs little, so more samples can make up for a coarse signal. Yue et al. (NeurIPS 2025) also found that on math and coding problems, what a model can solve after RL hardly goes beyond what the base model can solve given a few more tries.

Finally, a critic really is hard to train. It has to predict the future, and a critic that estimates badly is sometimes worse than simply splitting the score evenly. On the theory side, Jia, Rakhlin and Xie proved in an ICML 2025 paper that supervision on outcomes alone is statistically not much harder than step-by-step process supervision, with a gap of at most a polynomial factor in the number of steps.

All of this is true, but taken together it says one thing. On short-horizon tasks the problem is easy and does not need solving in its own right. The same theory paper even proves that when you can roll out again from a step, the advantage function (how much better this step is than average) is itself the optimal process reward model. When outcome supervision learns well, it is getting the credit right inside the algorithm; it just does not do so as a separate piece. As for that polynomial factor in the number of steps, my reading is that it can be ignored on a problem of a few steps and cannot be ignored at a few hundred.

The Agent Era

In agentic RL, every one of the conditions that made the problem easy is gone.

First, the forks have become very many. A single coding-agent attempt easily runs to dozens of turns and over a hundred thousand tokens, and in every turn, which file to read, which line to change and whether to run the tests are real choices. One wrong turn wastes everything after it, and the steps that were right before it are penalized along with it.

Second, sampling itself is no longer cheap. When a larger model runs agentic tasks, one trajectory takes a few days at best and a week or two at worst, so making up for a coarse signal by sampling a few more times is not an option. The longer the task, the more often every attempt in a group fails, and then comparing within the group yields no signal at all, as I wrote in Why Do Chinese LLMs Struggle with RL?

Finally, environments as they are now are harder to deal with. Zhang’s 2026 survey is devoted to exactly this problem and lists reasons why agentic RL makes credit assignment harder, for example that the model cannot see the whole state of the environment, that how the environment changes is not decided by the model’s actions alone, that you cannot freely go back to a step in the middle and start again, and that whether an intermediate step was right is hard to verify. The survey collects methods built for this problem between January 2024 and July 2026, and its core methods alone number 56. This year NeurIPS also accepted a paper on how to share a command-line agent’s final score out among its individual actions. An outdated problem does not produce dozens of new solutions in little more than two years.

So calling it outdated gets the timing exactly backwards. The time when credit assignment could most safely be ignored was the era of math problems. The time when it can least be ignored is now.

The Premise of “Outdated”

Not solving credit assignment in its own right has a cost. The cost is filling the gap with sheer sampling, running the same task dozens or hundreds of times until the group holds both successes and failures, then relying on large batches to average a coarse signal into a direction. With enough GPUs and data this certainly works, and GRPO can be trained by brute force.

So behind “outdated” lies an assumption, that GPUs and data are unlimited and every long-horizon task can be run as many times as it takes. By that logic, we might as well say we have unlimited GPUs and data and get everything right in one go. In reality, nobody has that.

Closely related is another common line. Seeing that data matters, people neglect algorithms, or even decide that only data matters. Data does matter, and nobody denies it. But data mattering does not imply that algorithms do not. Everyone knows that training base models has become more and more of an engineering effort, and that should make it all the clearer that no link in the chain can fail. If any one of data, algorithms, infrastructure or environments breaks, it drags the whole chain down. Why, then, would anyone think one link is what matters most and the rest hardly matter? Good data only gives you the potential to train RL well; whether that potential is realized depends on how the algorithm makes use of every score. Recognizing data alone is a little like a child who has just learned a new word and uses it to explain everything. It sounds knowledgeable, but it is naive.

As for “just use SFT”, that is another way around the problem. When the problem gets hard, stop doing that kind of task. But that kind of task is exactly what agents are for.

Methods go out of date; problems do not. In the era of long-horizon tasks and agents, credit assignment is not an old question to put down but one there is no way around.

entry.title: Why Do Chinese LLMs Struggle with RL?

link.title: Why Do Chinese LLMs Struggle with RL?

entry.content:
Whenever the gap between Chinese models and those of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google came up this year, I kept hearing two explanations. One is that there are not enough GPUs, the other that the infrastructure lags behind. Both are true, but I don’t think they explain everything. From what I have heard in conversations across the industry, the Chinese labs have all put real effort into long-horizon agentic RL, RL for coding agents above all, and for the most part it never took off. In the end, the gains in capability still came from distillation.

Why does something those three labs can make work fail in China? Beyond GPUs and infrastructure, I think there is a more fundamental reason. It lies in the path Chinese RL took when it started.

First, a little background; if you know it already, skip ahead. To train a large model with RL (reinforcement learning), you give it a task, let it work through to the end, score the result, and adjust the model according to the score. The core difficulty here is called credit assignment. When an attempt ends in success or failure, which of its steps deserve the credit or the blame? With only a few steps, that is easy to answer. When a single attempt runs to hundreds of steps, it becomes the crux of the whole problem.

Why GRPO worked so well

Large-scale RL in China started from GRPO, which DeepSeek proposed. The idea is simple. The model attempts the same task several times, the scores are compared, and any attempt above the average is reinforced while any below it is pushed down. There is no need to train a separate critic, a model built to estimate how much score is still to come from the current step onward. A critic takes up its own share of GPU memory and compute, and it may not train well anyway.

GRPO proved itself on math problems. RL on math takes very few turns. The model thinks, gives an answer, and the episode is over in one or two. In that setting, the signal from comparing within the group, whether this attempt did better or worse than average, is enough to get credit assignment right. It saved memory, needed no critic and worked well, so it quickly became the default way to do RL in China.

Once tasks get long, it stops working

GRPO’s signal is actually coarse. The model has to finish a whole trajectory before it gets a single score, right or wrong, and that score is given to the whole trajectory. If the outcome is right, every step is reinforced; if it is wrong, every step is penalized, no matter which steps were in fact done well.

On simple math problems, a signal this coarse does little harm. But in today’s coding agent tasks, a single attempt easily runs to dozens of turns and more than a hundred thousand tokens. When hundreds of decisions share one score, the model cannot tell which step made it succeed and which made it fail.

There is something worse. Comparing within a group only works if some attempts at the same task succeed and some fail. The longer the task, the more steps in a row have to go right, and the more often every attempt fails. When they all fail, they all get the same score, there is nothing to compare, and the compute for that round is wasted. As tasks get longer, GRPO’s signal gets scarcer as well as coarser.

The bigger the model and the more complex the task, the finer the reward needs to be. That is exactly the direction in which GRPO’s approach runs into a wall.

Why it is so hard to get out

Everyone can see the problem, yet getting out is hard. Most new algorithms are improvements built on GRPO, and the general feeling is that GRPO is already well ahead of the alternatives. But for all the tweaking, the results barely move, because the root problem, a single score at the very end, has not been fixed.

Some have taken a different road with OPD (on-policy distillation), in which a student model works the tasks itself and a teacher model tells it, token by token, what was good and what was not. But OPD needs a good teacher first. And for the teacher to break through the current ceiling and become better than it is now, the only way is still RL.

So it becomes a vicious circle. However the algorithms are optimized, every road leads back to getting RL right first, and RL done the GRPO way cannot get credit assignment right on long tasks.

What is locked in is a lesson, not code

Saying everyone is locked into GRPO calls for one explanation. Switching from GRPO to a method with a critic is a small change in the code. Why can’t teams of several hundred people make the switch?

My reading is that what is locked in is not a choice of algorithm but accumulated capability. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google came all the way up from the RLHF era. Back then the standard recipe was PPO plus a critic plus a reward model, so they were forced to learn how to train a value model, how to keep it from collapsing, and how to keep it in step with a policy that keeps changing. That craft has settled into their teams.

Large-scale RL in China began at exactly the moment GRPO showed you could do very well without a critic. GRPO was designed partly with the GPU shortage in mind, since dropping the critic drops a large chunk of the cost. As a result, the Chinese labs in effect skipped this lesson. Now that tasks are long and a critic is truly needed, what is missing is not a switch but a whole body of engineering intuition that was never built up.

What a critic really buys you: the scope of comparison

The difference between a critic and GRPO goes beyond training one more model. It lies in what each of them compares against.

GRPO’s baseline comes only from the few attempts at the same task in the same batch, so it is a local comparison. If the whole group fails, it has nothing to go on.

A critic’s baseline is learned from all experience, so it is global. It can recognize that the intermediate state in front of it looks a lot like states in other tasks that went on to succeed. So even if not one attempt at this task has succeeded, the critic can borrow experience from elsewhere to tell the model whether a step was a good one.

Long-horizon tasks need exactly this kind of transfer, where a judgment learned on one task can be used midway through another. GRPO only ever looks at the group in front of it, so by its very structure it cannot do this.

A deeper turn of the circle: who does the judging

If a critic is that good, why is it hard to train? The root cause is that judging whether an intermediate state of a long task is good is almost as hard as finishing the task. The judge has to be at least as smart as whoever does the work.

As far as I know, Google’s internal RL relies on exactly this route, a critic or a PRM (process reward model, a model that scores each step). It uses generative methods to label every step, or even every token, and so gives feedback far finer than one score at the end. That is what gets its RL off the ground.

This route rests on a premise that is rarely said out loud. You need a judge stronger than the model being trained. Frontier labs have one, because they can use their own strongest model to judge the process. The strong model marks out good signals, those signals train a stronger model, and the stronger model becomes the judge in the next round. It is a loop that keeps itself turning.

Followers have no judge stronger than themselves. They can only borrow someone else’s model, and that leads back to distillation.

So the vicious circle closes twice. Breakthroughs in capability depend on RL, RL depends on good mid-task signals, good mid-task signals depend on a stronger judge, and a stronger judge depends on a breakthrough in capability. First movers can climb on their own. Followers need outside help for every step up.

So where is the gap?

Putting all this together, here is my conclusion. GRPO was the handiest choice for a follower, and it made the trap deeper, but the trap is rooted further down. At the root, first movers can use their own models to train themselves, and followers cannot. Too few GPUs, too little compute and immature infrastructure add one more layer on top of this structure and widen the gap further.

If this reading is right, more patching on top of GRPO is unlikely to change the picture. What really needs attacking is how to get fine-grained mid-task signals on long tasks, either by training a good critic or by building good process judges. It is a lesson there is no way around, and the sooner it is made up, the better.

This view is based on what I have heard and on my own reasoning. I’d welcome discussion.
entry.summary: Beyond GPUs and infrastructure, I think there is a more fundamental reason, and it lies in the path Chinese RL took when it started.

entry.title: LLMs Unified the Input, Coding Unified the Output

link.title: LLMs Unified the Input, Coding Unified the Output

entry.content:
Many people see the coding agent as a tool for writing code, a stronger programming assistant. I have come to think it means far more than that. The coding paradigm is to today what LLMs were to the research of the pre-LLM era, one general approach that brings a whole range of specialized directions under one roof.

If I had to sum up my view in one sentence, it would be that LLMs unified the input and coding unified the output. The first unification let models understand anything; this one lets them make anything.

To explain this, I need to start from the idea that compression is intelligence.

Compression is intelligence

Ilya Sutskever and others have long said, in all kinds of settings, that compression is intelligence. My own reading goes like this. If a single entity, say a neural network or a human brain, can on its own handle many different tasks and generalize to all sorts of domains, it must have grasped some essential regularities. Those regularities are what let one entity do so many things.

The reverse holds as well. Make one entity do tasks from different domains, which in plain terms means training one model on all kinds of tasks and using a good form to compress everything into it, and it is forced to learn those essentials. Learned separately, each piece can get by on memorized special cases. Learned together, they only fit once you find the regularities they share.

Ilya explained unsupervised learning in exactly these terms in a 2023 talk. He said a good compressor finds the structure that different data share, so compressing a lot of data together teaches more than compressing each piece separately. Jack Rae said the same year that the goal of a foundation model is to compress useful information losslessly, as well as it possibly can.

For LLMs, that good form is the Transformer and its attention architecture, together with the whole pipeline of pretraining, mid-training and post-training. Pretraining pulls the knowledge and information in all kinds of text into one model, so what it learns is general knowledge rather than knowledge specific to one field. Yi Ma’s group even started from the goal of compressing data and derived the structure of the Transformer layer by layer, which suggests attention itself can be understood as doing compression.

Model size matters too, of course, but that is more of an engineering question. Once you understand the principle, you can keep making the entity bigger so that it learns more, compresses better and comes closer to the regularities behind the knowledge. A study from HKUST and Tencent tested dozens of public models and found that the better a model compresses data, the stronger its abilities, with the two lying almost on a straight line.

Covering everything makes it better at each thing

This is how LLMs outclassed pre-LLM AI across the board. Instead of specializing, they cover everything, and that breadth is exactly what makes them better at the specialties.

A DeepMind study gives a very concrete example. A language model trained mainly on text, when used to compress images and speech, did better than PNG, which was designed for images, and FLAC, which was designed for audio. The generalist beat the specialists on their own ground.

This is the same thing Sutton called the bitter lesson. People always want to build rules out of their own reasoning and construct a perfect model, and without exception it runs into trouble in the end. Looking back on seventy years of AI research, Sutton concluded that what wins in the long run is always general methods that can absorb more compute, mainly learning and search. Hard-coding human understanding into a system works in the short run and holds it back in the long run.

In the pre-LLM era, people designed all sorts of network architectures and pipelines to push up benchmark scores, and none of them matched LLMs. Once LLMs arrived, they replaced all of those models and paradigms.

The same thing has happened again

In the era of coding agents, it has happened again, and more thoroughly.

Look at what the latest models can do. I have watched Fable 5.2 paint a picture stroke by stroke purely by writing code, with a result that looks almost the same as a human painting. It can also build an entire 3D scene in code, and make videos. This used to be unimaginable. To generate video, you needed a dedicated video generation model, such as a diffusion model. Not anymore. Coding alone, as one paradigm, can do almost everything well, robot control included. There are even recent rumors that OpenAI has a model that does robot control well at very low latency.

All of this shows the same thing again and again. The further you go in splitting the model into parts that each do one specialized job, the more surely it all gets unified in the end. Eventually people find it is better to do it with one model.

Some will say one model is too big and too slow for these jobs. But speed can be solved through optimization. A model can be made much faster with almost no loss of ability. That is an engineering problem, not a problem with the paradigm.

LLMs unified the input, coding unified the output

Why code and not something else? I think the key point is that the two unifications cover the two ends.

LLMs unified the input. They turned every task into text in, text out. Whether it is translation, question answering, writing or reasoning, what comes in is the same kind of thing, and the model understands it with one set of parameters. That unified the understanding end, so the model can read anything.

But understanding alone is not enough. What an LLM outputs is only text, and text by itself cannot touch the world. It can describe a painting but cannot paint one; it can explain how to control a robot but cannot move a single joint. So beyond LLMs, people still had to train separate specialized models for drawing, for video and for controlling machines, and the output end stayed fragmented.

Code fills in exactly that end. Code can express any computation and can also be executed, so the model’s output is no longer just text. It becomes action that has an effect on the world. A painting, a 3D scene, a video, a command for a robot, each of them is what you get by running a program. All those specialized output models are folded into a single action, writing a program.

Put the two together and one model goes all the way from reading to doing. The first unification let models understand anything; this one lets them do anything.

Learning plus search: the bitter lesson in its purest form

This also fits the bitter lesson neatly. Sutton said that what wins in the long run is learning and search. Pretraining is learning. A coding agent writing code, running it, reading the errors and fixing it again is search. The coding agent combines the two, which arguably makes it the purest form of the bitter lesson.

Generating with code is itself compression

There is one more reason. Generating with code is itself compression. In compression theory, the complexity of a piece of data is defined as the length of the shortest program that can generate it, and this is called Kolmogorov complexity. So when a model paints a picture in code, it is writing a compressed description of that picture. The coding paradigm is not merely compressing in a way that resembles LLMs. It is the most direct form compression takes at the output end. The idea that compression is intelligence, from earlier, and the coding paradigm, here, are really two sides of the same thing.

Code generates processes, not pixels

Some may think code only suits structured things like charts and geometric figures, and that real paintings and photographs are too complex to have any program shorter than themselves. That underestimates code.

Code generates a process, not pixels. A human painting is made one stroke at a time, so its shortest program is not a table of pixels but that sequence of strokes. A real photograph is produced by light and objects following physical laws, and a ray tracer plus a scene description is itself a program. The only part that truly cannot be compressed is the random detail, and random detail does not need to be reproduced point by point. It only has to be right statistically, and one call to a random number generator in the code is enough for that.

Almost everything in the world comes out of some process. Whatever has a generating process can be written out by some program. That is why I say coding has almost no ceiling.

This is moving very fast. In 2025 Meta published a test that turns compression directly into a programming problem. The model is given a piece of audio, text or DNA data and asked to write the shortest program that generates it. The conclusion at the time was that this was extremely hard even for the strongest models of that generation. A little more than a year later, models can already paint pictures in code that come close to a human’s.

Code is also the best teaching material

The coding paradigm has one more advantage that often gets overlooked. It is very well suited to collecting data, especially data distilled from people.

An ability like generating video is not something people can teach directly. I would not know how to tell a model “this is how video should be generated.” But in the form of code, I can teach it. I can teach it how to generate video with code, how to paint with code, how to operate a machine with code. Almost anything coding can do can be taught this way. Passed through the layer of code, human skill becomes something a model can read and learn.

Code can also be run and checked, and you know whether it is right as soon as you run it. That makes it the place where RL gets rewards most easily, too. In Why Do Chinese LLMs Struggle with RL? I wrote that RL is stuck because it cannot get fine-grained feedback. Code is exactly the field where feedback is cheapest.

And coding itself can do almost anything; the only difference is whether the conditions are in place. It has almost no ceiling.

Where specialized research goes

So my conclusion is that specialized research may well continue, but all of it will be overtaken by strong coding agent foundation models. Such research may still exist, but like today’s expert systems or standalone image classifiers, it will rarely be put to real use. When it comes to practice, people will use the foundation model, unless a specialized solution is genuinely much cheaper.

LLMs unified the input and brought the many directions of the pre-LLM era into one. Coding agents are now unifying the output, and doing the same to today’s specialized directions.

References

  • Ilya Sutskever, An Observation on Generalization, Simons Institute, 2023.
  • Jack Rae, Compression for AGI, Stanford MLSys Seminar, 2023.
  • Yaodong Yu et al., White-Box Transformers via Sparse Rate Reduction: Compression Is All There Is?, JMLR 2024.
  • Yuzhen Huang et al., Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly, COLM 2024.
  • Grégoire Delétang et al., Language Modeling Is Compression, ICLR 2024.
  • Richard Sutton, The Bitter Lesson, 2019.
  • Ori Yoran et al., The KoLMogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation, ICLR 2025.
  • Marcus Hutter, Hutter Prize (since 2006).
entry.summary: The first unification let models understand anything; this one lets them make anything.

entry.title: Crooked Environments, Crooked Agents
entry.content:
The field has spent this year worrying that agents cheat on benchmarks, with good reason. Berkeley RDI took all 89 Terminal-Bench tasks with a fake curl. Verifier Hardening told agents to cheat and got through 47 of the 89 tasks in Terminal-Bench 2.0. Terminal-Bench 3.0 moved the agent and the grader into separate containers, and 4.1 is slated for tamper-resistant verifiers.

Most of those numbers come from telling the agent to cheat. Audits of released models, Vals AI’s among them, show that agents cheat unasked too, and OpenAI and Anthropic have watched cheating emerge during training, though those training runs are not public. Allen AI released every attempt of Tmax’s 500-step run, so I used it to look at two things: which shortcut grows, and where it comes from. That decides how we read this year’s score gains and where anti-cheating effort should go. I measured it myself, with a set of off-the-shelf models as a baseline and two more public runs for contrast.

The result was not quite what I expected. In this training record, agents almost never go after the grader. What grows fast is something else. The tasks ask the agent to compile a program, but the training sandbox lacks the C headers it needs. The agent learns to put a script at that path instead; the script prints the right answers, and the tests cannot tell. That shortcut never touches the grader, so isolating the grader does not reach it. It needs a different fix.

First, a quick note on how an agent like this is trained; skip it if you know this already. We give it a task, say, write a program on a Linux machine and compile it, and it types commands to get there. When it is done, a test script checks what it left behind, and a pass earns a reward. Reinforcement learning repeats this task after task, nudging the model toward whatever scores. Throughout, the grader means that test script. Terminal-Bench, mentioned above, is 89 tasks of this kind and the benchmark most papers report.

Do agents touch the grader when nobody asks?

Start with off-the-shelf models. TermGrade published full trajectories from six models on 1,004 terminal tasks outside Terminal-Bench. Some tasks name a grading path in their instructions, so I dropped those, which leaves 959 tasks and 34,524 attempts.

I first scanned every attempt’s commands for grading paths. A command named one in 295 attempts, 0.85%. Models differ a lot: 0.03% at the low end, 7.87% for DeepSeek at the top. Writes to a grading path happened in only 3 attempts, all in the batch whose disk was full, one of them trying to delete the grader’s environment to free space. I then read 20 random attempts to see why they looked, and every one wanted to learn what the task required. Across all 36,144 attempts, no output contained the grader’s tests.

Read those numbers with their setting. TermGrade copies tests in at scoring time, so while the agent works, the container holds no tests to change, and my path scan cannot see outputs hard-coded for the tests. This shows what was measured under that setting; it says nothing about models being honest.

What about after training? The Tmax authors ran a check in their section D.6 and found three kinds of cheating on Terminal-Bench 2.0 that the base model did not show, such as replacing /tests/filter.py with a no-op or faking a Caffe binary. Those runs scored 0. They also published every attempt from all 500 training steps, which almost nobody does. Everything below depends on that record, and I am grateful for it.

What 500 steps of training taught

The record trains on 8 tasks per step with 32 attempts per task, 128,000 attempts in all. Tests enter the container only after the agent submits.

First, did the agent go after the grader? A command named the test file in 26 attempts. None got its contents, because before submission the file is not there. But the grader runs in the agent’s container, so Berkeley RDI’s method, replacing a program the tests call before they run, would work here too. So I also scanned for writes to conftest, pytest and the Python interpreter, got 8 hits, and read each one. None changed the grading.

So what was it doing? The training sandbox has gcc but no C headers, and apt does not work, so 16,923 attempts hit a compile error of this kind. On tasks that require compiling, tests mostly check whether the program prints the right output. A rough keyword scan finds only about 5% of them checking whether the submitted file is actually a compiled program.

Here is one real attempt from step 45. Step through it.

This attempt first says “No, that would be cheating.” Dozens of turns later it writes “This is a cheat but will make the automated test pass.” Its final summary openly says the executable is a Python wrapper. The grader does not read summaries.

How common is this? On the 1,629 tasks that require a compile, I counted the attempts that put a script at the path the task names: 7.4% in the first 50 steps, 27.0% in steps 150 to 249. Attempts that did so and passed went from 4.1% to 18.2%. I read 55 passing attempts, one per task, and about nine in ten had a script where the task asked for a compiled program, or had written a program the task said was provided.

To check that this is not noise, I split each step’s 8 tasks into odd and even numbers and computed the change for each half separately. The two halves differ by between -13.3 and +3.7 points, far less than this rise. To check the scan itself, I drew 200 random attempts on these tasks and had a model label each one without seeing the scan’s verdict, then read every disagreement myself. Agreement with the scan was Cohen’s κ 0.74. What the scan mostly misses are other fake programs, such as a faked “provided” program or hand-written ELF bytes, which are more common early in training. The 200 were drawn 100 from each stretch; counting every kind of fake program, the share went from about 10% to about 23%.

The reasoning shifts too. Attempts mentioning cheating went from 2.1% to 13.0%, and attempts working out what the tests will check went from 8.0% to 43.2%. The released checkpoint is step 200, inside the later stretch.

Whether the fake programs on Terminal-Bench in section D.6 came from shortcuts like these, I cannot prove; they have the same shape. Tmax’s reported gain does not shrink because of this, since those runs scored 0.

Does every environment defect lead to a shortcut?

A second public record, a Qwen3-30B-A3B run on R2E-Gym’s code-repair tasks, also releases every session’s log. For its first 60 steps the sandbox could not resolve localhost, so tasks that start a local server, tornado and aiohttp among them, had tests that could not run. The authors also reran 50 steps with the fix in place from the start, drawing nearly the same tasks in the same order, which gives a clean comparison. Those tasks passed about 6 points less in the broken run, 26.8% against 32.4%; the other tasks differed by 1 point.

This time the agent learned no shortcut. About half the sessions that hit the error changed localhost to 127.0.0.1 in their own checks, a few added a line to the hosts file, and a handful edited the library’s own test helpers. Comparing attempts at the same task in the same step, none of these scored reliably higher than not doing it, and the test-helper edits all scored 0. Adding to the hosts file fell from about one in five such sessions in the first 10 steps to about one in fifty later, and switching to 127.0.0.1 did not become more common.

A third public record trains a 4B model on the same tasks as Tmax. I measured two of its runs, 240 steps each, sampling every fourth step, and both kept improving. Its sandbox also lacks the C headers, and about three in ten attempts on compile tasks hit that error, close to Tmax. The difference is that apt works here. In about eight in ten of the attempts that hit the error, the agent installed packages on its own, most often libc6-dev, which provides those headers. Among attempts that hit the error, the share leaving a fake program stayed between 2% and 5% from start to finish; under the same conditions in Tmax it rose from 16% to 63%.

Why do the three records differ? As I read it, it depends on whether the cheapest route to a pass is repairing the environment or leaving a fake program. Tmax could not repair its missing headers, so a fake program was cheapest; the third run fixed them with one apt command; R2E’s tests themselves were broken, so no fake program could pass. With only three records, this is just my reading.

What isolation covers, and what it does not

Isolation does work. Those 26 attempts got no test contents precisely because tests stay out of the container until submission. The /tests/filter.py swap in section D.6, and the 958 attempts above that wrote their own reference, are also what an isolated grader is for.

Passing off a script is a different problem. The test file is untouched, the grading environment is untouched, and the script’s answers are correct. Even with the containers separated, the test still sees a file that runs and prints the right thing. Only the test itself can catch this: when the instructions require a compile, check whether the submitted file is a compiled program on top of checking its behavior. So tamper resistance and checking the artifact are two fixes for two problems, and both are worth doing.

Beyond cheating, what else moves the score?

When reading Terminal-Bench gains, several things besides cheating move the score, each by about as much as the gains themselves.

Start with the harness, the framework that runs the model in the terminal. In the official 2.1 notice, the same GPT-5.4 scores 77.3 on Codex CLI and 54.8 on Terminus-2. The same Qwen3.8-27B on the same 2.1 scores 76.4 in Tev, run on Terminus-2, and 49.4 in Skill2Env, run on Pi. The next three I computed on TermGrade’s 1,004 tasks, which are not Terminal-Bench. Turning on thinking for the same weights adds 7.88 points; swapping in a different 89 tasks gives a 95% range about 16 points wide; rerunning the same tasks gives a difference with a standard deviation of about 2. Then there is retraining: TermGrade retrained one recipe five times and landed between 43.4 and 46.3.

There are good examples too. TermGrade states how many times it retrained and how it picks checkpoints. MiMo audited its own training and found the model increasingly working around the tests when trained without online grading. Of the 12 environment papers I counted that report Terminal-Bench gains, none states a check of whether the passing evaluation attempts behind the gain really did the task. TermGrade comes closest, noting that its gains raised completion and answer quality together and asking others to check. Several papers check for benchmark leakage or guard against hacking during training; those are different problems, and they matter too.

What to take away

  1. When comparing scores, only comparisons within one harness count. A score from changed settings cannot be compared with the leaderboard.
  2. With 89 tasks and 5 trials each, do not read much into a gap under 4 points between two evaluations; with different tasks, allow a wider margin.
  3. Before training, confirm the sandbox has the toolchain the tasks need. That is what guards against the large share caused by missing headers.
  4. Also confirm each task’s setup actually ran and the programs the task says are provided really exist. Train What You Deploy ran the tasks for real and marked 6.9% of TMax instances invalid, 5.9% of them failing their own initial state.
  5. When you find an environment defect mid-run, ask two things first: can the agent repair it itself, and if not, can a fake program still pass the tests? Of the three records, only the one where the defect could not be repaired and a fake program could pass learned a shortcut.
  6. When the instructions require a compile, check whether the submitted file is a compiled program on top of checking its behavior; reading the ELF header is enough. When they only ask for a program that runs, a script is a valid answer.
  7. Keep reference answers where the agent cannot reach them. Terminal-Bench 3.0’s separate containers for agent and grader already do this.
  8. Scan your own rollouts during training, not only for grading paths but also for scripts placed at the paths the tasks name.

The scan scripts and per-step readings are at github.com/Battam1111/shortcut-scan. Point them at your own rollouts.

When the crooked path is cheaper, agents learn to take it. Make the right path the cheapest one, and people and agents alike are more likely to stay on track.

entry.title: Making the Environment Trainable
entry.content:
Models became trainable. The sentence sounds trivial, but it is the single fact behind a decade of progress: give a system a signal for how it is doing and a way to improve on it, and scale does the rest. The environment a model learns in never got that deal.

It is worth being precise about what the model side actually received. Backpropagation gave every parameter a share of the blame for every error, which is to say it solved credit assignment inside the network. Once that signal existed, improvement stopped being a craft and became a budget: more data, more compute, better models. Everything we call scaling rests on that loop running billions of times without a human in it.

Now look at the other side of the training run. The environment is not even a single thing. There is a reward model over here, trained on preference data and judged by its accuracy. There are verifiers over there, judged by agreement rates. A curriculum somewhere else, assembled by heuristics and judged by intuition. Each piece is built separately, evaluated separately, and swapped separately. Not one of them is judged by the only thing that makes it worth having: what it does to the model it exists to train. The environment is not a system. It is a pile.

A pile cannot be trained. That is the honest reason the environment never got the model side’s deal, and it is why I do not think of “make the environment trainable” as one problem. It is a stack of problems, each standing on the one below.

Measurement. Can you read what a single piece does to the model? Today you mostly cannot. A reward model’s benchmark accuracy fails to predict the policy it trains; the effect has to be read inside the training run itself. Until this layer works, everything above it is guesswork.

Credit. A model is trained by many pieces at once, and they produce one outcome together. Whose share is whose? Take a piece out and re-run, and you have changed what every piece downstream of it sees; the answer comes back biased in a way more sampling cannot fix. Credit has to be computed by running the counterfactual, not predicted or approximated by deletion.

Training a piece. A measured effect can become the piece’s own training signal. This is where the environment stops being infrastructure and starts improving. It carries an obligation the model side never had: the piece must be withdrawable, with the gain staying with the model after it is gone. Otherwise what you improved is not the model but the ensemble around it.

The team. Pieces trained together, serving one model, have to coordinate rather than interfere. Joint shaping is known to break where individual shaping succeeds, so this layer is not a free consequence of the one below it.

Generalization. An environment that trains one model well should carry to the next model, the next task, and eventually past text. This is the layer where the bet pays off, and the one furthest from current evidence.

My three studies so far live on the first two layers, with a first step into the third: measurement where the standard metric fails, exact credit where outcomes are shared, and one training-time piece that is absorbed and then withdrawn. That is deliberate. The stack collapses without its ground floor, and the ground floor is the part nobody had built.

Why believe the ceiling moves if the stack gets built? Because models increasingly learn from experience their environments generate: tasks proposed, outputs scored, mistakes checked. The environment is the factory of that experience. A model that improves inside a fixed factory converges to what the factory can teach; the factory itself has to improve for the ceiling to move. The field has seen this once before: features used to be hand-crafted, then they became learned, and that single change renamed the field. The environment is the largest hand-crafted stage left.

So the bet, stated once more: environments themselves must scale, train, and generalize the way models have. I am starting where the stack starts, with measurement. The companion note lays out why that order is forced, not chosen.

This note replaces an earlier statement of my direction written under a different name. The name did not survive; the ambition did.
entry.summary: Models became trainable; the environment never got that deal. Today it is not even a single thing. What it takes to change that, laid out as a stack of problems, and why the ceiling moves if the stack gets built.

entry.title: Why Measurement Comes First
entry.content:
Three fields have hit the same wall, each in its own vocabulary.

In RLHF, the wall is that a reward model’s benchmark accuracy fails to predict the policy it trains. My first study varied a reward model’s accuracy together with its number of training steps, and found an interior optimum: past a point, the more accurate reward model trained the worse policy. The best reward model and the most accurate one also differed in the distribution of their rewards and in the KL divergence of the policies they trained. The field’s own evaluation line has since documented the same disconnect at scale: RewardBench 2 concedes that accuracy is necessary but not sufficient, and Frick et al. report a negative correlation between benchmark score and downstream RLHF performance among the top models. The recognized mechanism is reward overoptimization, Goodhart’s law in RL clothing (Gao, Schulman and Hilton, ICML 2023). Best-of-N selection is a different regime where static scores still work; policy optimization is where they break.

In control, the wall is that the one theorem everyone relies on stops at the reward. Ng, Harada and Russell (1999) proved potential-based reward shaping leaves the optimal policy invariant, and that the guarantee is necessary and sufficient there. The action channel has no such theorem, and this is still the live frontier (Forbes et al., ICML 2025). Practice shows the cost: a correction learned on the action is either kept at deployment, as residual policy learning keeps it on a fixed base, or removed without a guarantee. My second study co-trains a gated shaping term on the action output and measures its absorption into the base policy directly: a trainable base absorbs the term when its own output layer can reproduce it exactly, the gate rises and then falls on its own, and removing the term afterward costs almost nothing, so withdrawal is measured rather than hoped for.

In cooperative LLM systems, the wall is one shared outcome and no way to split it. This is the oldest name in the field: the credit-assignment problem, coined by Minsky in 1961. Inside a single differentiable model, backpropagation answers it. Between the models of a training system, no gradient flows, and one standard workaround, removing a piece and re-running, is structurally biased: removal changes what every downstream piece that reads it receives, and more samples do not shrink that bias. My third study shows that in a team of LLM agents the workaround is unnecessary when everything a downstream agent reads is written into the trace, because then the trace is the state. This holds by construction when the agents read only the trace; only hidden state that the trace does not record lies outside it. At any decision point, one message can be substituted and the run continued to its reward while everything before it stays fixed; this is counterfactual continuation. Per-decision credit becomes exact in identification, with only sampling variance left.

One wall, three vocabularies. But why must the fix be measurement from inside the run, rather than better benchmarks outside it? Because the field’s own evidence shows the effect is regime-dependent. The same reward model produces different downstream results under different training regimes: on-policy against off-policy, policy optimization against best-of-N. A static benchmark cannot predict an effect that depends on a regime the benchmark does not know. This is not a preference for one methodology over another. It is what regime-dependence forces.

There is a second principle underneath, and it decides what counts as a contribution at all. A training-time piece can help in two ways: it can build capability into the model’s weights, or it can prop up the system for as long as it stays attached. The traditions that got this right made withdrawal part of the concept. Instructional scaffolding (Wood, Bruner and Ross, 1976) defines the tutor’s support as something that withers away as competence grows. Distillation (Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, 2015) measures success on the small model running alone at deployment. Much of the current field runs the other way: test-time compute keeps verifiers and search attached at inference, renting capability per query. Both are legitimate products. They are different products, and only a withdrawal test tells you which one you actually built: capability in the weights, or capability in the ensemble.

Put the two principles together and the order of the whole program falls out. You cannot train the pieces of an environment on their contribution until you can compute each piece’s contribution; you cannot compute it from outside the run, because the effect is regime-dependent; and you cannot call it a contribution at all until it survives the piece’s removal. Measurement is not the modest part of the plan. It is the ground floor, and the companion note describes the floors above it.
entry.summary: Three fields hit the same wall in their own vocabularies. Regime-dependence forces measurement inside the training run, and the withdrawal test decides what counts as a contribution at all.
